Geometry reference rows re-captured on 2026-11-12, with sign-off.

What moved, and why. Each was a change made on purpose on the branch
feat/materials-optics; the record hashes a thing's looks as well as its
shape, so a new look moves a row as surely as a new shape does.

- webb, eight rows, in spacecraft-reference-arm64.txt. Its mirrors
  became gold and its sunshield aluminium, from the metals' published
  optical constants (f4dd2058). Then its shape was rebuilt by its
  papers: the bus under the shield, the tower, the instrument module,
  the solar array, the antenna, the secondary at 7.169 m (cb53d7a0).
- mcrn-larson, eight rows, in saucer-reference-arm64.txt. Its portholes
  were given a glow of their own and it was given named lamps
  (99b25f9a). An earlier commit on this branch said its records would
  not move. That was wrong.
- mcrn-larson-landed, eight rows, new, in saucer-reference-arm64.txt.
  The kind was added on this branch (aea6e978) and had no rows.

No other row moved. Before the re-capture the reference test failed on
webb's eight and mcrn-larson's eight and on nothing else, and said the
landed kind had no reference.

How. The producer, run at af922bbf with the tree otherwise clean:

    GOWORK=off go run ./manufacture/testdata/geometry_sample.go

It printed 776 rows: the 768 recorded, and the landed Larson's eight.
The 24 rows above were copied from its output into the two files, and
then compared with its output again: byte for byte the same.
geometry-records.yaml's totals went from 768 cases and 606 geometries to
776 and 614; the 162 refusals did not change.

Webb's eight rows were captured a second time the same morning, after
its sun side was built from NASA's picture of it (the pallets, the
booms, the row of five solar panels, the radiators, the round
interface, the flap). The producer was run again on that tree; nothing
but webb's rows differed from the first run, and webb's eight on disk
are that second run's, byte for byte.

The files after:

    92438268bca1b19928eecdd89d9b8f6f1b5d3a620191641d5260ef616bebf949  saucer-reference-arm64.txt
    ef1dde0ebcc9aa37859cc71ab73dd0da7ddb51a8d2cc2b479c7b1f66b6b5ef35  spacecraft-reference-arm64.txt

The spacecraft file's checksum above is its sixth capture's, the
latest: the sixth followed when the sun-facing membrane was given its
seams, and again nothing but webb's rows differed from the run before.
The fifth followed when the shield's layers were fanned, close
at the middle and apart at the edges. That change was made in the
plate every kind's flat plates are made of; the producer's whole output
was compared with the run before, and nothing but webb's rows differed. A fourth capture of webb's eight followed the third, when its
sunshield's outline became a kite with scalloped edges and its solar
panels were sized to sit inside it. Nothing but webb's rows differed
from the run before.

A third capture of webb's eight, the same morning. The secondary's two
numbers were moved into the research file as the paper's page has them,
in millimetres, so the project's own check can hold them to the page.
Dividing by a thousand in a different place moved the secondary by a
rounding of the last bit, and the rows with it. Nothing but webb's rows
differed from the second run.

What this does not do. spacecraft-reference-provenance.json still
describes the first capture: its base commit, its reference checksum
and its list of source checksums are that capture's, and are now out of
date for webb's rows. It was left as the record of what it records.
What these rows prove is what the record always proved: that the things
are built the same from one run to the next. They do not prove the
things are right.
